newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania says JP Morgan to lead $200 mln Eurobond.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania says JP Morgan to lead $200 mln Eurobond.

text.p: Lithuania said on Friday that it had appointed JP Morgan Securities to lead a $200 million Eurobond issue and to act as the country's ratings adviser.
"The proposals were very competitive and demonstrate strong support for Lithuania from international banks," Lithuanian Finance Minister Algirdas Shemeta said in a statement.
"We believe JP Morgan will do the best job for us, but are also expecting continued support from the other banks (who applied for this issue)," he said.
This would be Lithuania's benchmark debut bond issue in the Eurodollar market, the finance ministry said.
The ministry said that 22 major international banks responded to Lithuania's invitation for proposals.
Lithuania plans to seek a rating from U.S. credit ratings agency Standard & Poor's before it launches the Eurobond.
"Depending on the result (of the S&P rating) and on general developments in the Eurodollar bond market, Lithuania is looking to issue the bond later in the year," the statement said.
"We are not in a hurry, it's more important that we reach out and explain Lithuania's positive development and prospects for international investors," Shemeta said.
Lithuania made its debut on international capital markets in December 1995, with a $60 million Eurobond with a two year maturity and a 10 percent coupon.
That was later upgraded in August 1996 by $50 million.
In September last year U.S. based credit ratings agency Moody's assigned a Ba2 rating to Lithuania's foreign currency debt and a Ba3 to the country's bank deposits.

In January European credit rating agency IBCA assigned a BB plus long-term foreign currency rating to the Republic of Lithuania. It also assigned a short-term foreign currency rating of B and a rating of BBB plus for local currency-dominated government debt.
Under Lithuania's current budget law, the country's foreign debt cannot increase by more than $600 million this year.
The country's foreign currency debt at the end of 1996 stood at around $1.2 billion, or 16.3 percent of Gross Domestic Product.
Given the country's tight monetary and fiscal policies and its modest borrowing requirement, few analysts expect it to bring much paper to international capital markets.

"We will probably not go to the international capital markets more than two times this year," Ruta Skyriene, deputy director of the international department of Lithuania's ministry of finance, told Reuters.
